"Superposition" here is the term of art from Chris Olah and Anthropic's interpretability research — it names a specific strategy neurons can use to represent more distinct features than there are neurons available, by storing them as non-orthogonal directions in activation space rather than giving each feature its own dedicated neuron. The article's own worked example is the clearest way in: a code that can represent all colored shapes with only 4 neurons, "just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers," is what the piece calls dense or maximal superposition. Dense codes like this have a very cool advantage: they can represent far more, totally unrelated objects than there are neurons — but it isn't possible to generically select most colors or shapes with a linear probe, let alone sets, and a non-linearity is required to retrieve them once features are packed together this way.

The reason this trick works at all is sparsity: when features are dense (ie. combinations are common), networks can only represent one feature per neuron. But when features are sparse (combinations of many features are rare) superposition becomes possible. The article treats superposition as standing in direct opposition to "composition" (building objects out of independently-meaningful feature-neurons) — if one has m bits to encode stimuli... storing n features which arbitrarily compose together requires exp(n) volume; so we can only store fully composable features in m bits. But if there's no composition, one can instead store exp(m) items in superposition.

Although the article doesn't spell this out at the point where the word first appears, it's referring back to Anthropic's earlier paper *Toy Models of Superposition*, which the piece itself cites later as fundamentally exploring this trade-off, although it casts things in terms of an equivalent idea of feature sparsity rather than composition. answers.asked: An informal note on the relationship between superposition and distributed representations by Chris Olah.
answers.text:
The selection is simply naming the author, so the real question here is: who is Chris Olah, and what makes this piece his?

As you may know, Chris Olah is a machine learning researcher best known for pioneering work in neural network interpretability — the effort to understand what's actually happening inside neural networks rather than treating them as black boxes. He was one of the founders of Distill, the journal for clear visual explanations of ML research, and later worked at OpenAI and Google Brain on visualizing and understanding neural network features before co-founding Anthropic, where he leads interpretability research. The "Transformer Circuits Thread" mentioned at the top of this document is Anthropic's ongoing interpretability research series, of which this note is a part; the "original paper on superposition" it refers to is the earlier Anthropic work (Toy Models of Superposition) that this note is informally following up on.

That background matters for how to read the piece: it's framed explicitly as informal — a working researcher thinking out loud about a conceptual distinction (composition vs. superposition) that came up repeatedly in response to that earlier, more formal paper, rather than a polished result.

answers.asked: What does "superposition" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, "superposition" names one of the two things people conflate under "distributed representations" — the other being "composition." The article introduces this split directly: these two different notions of distributed representations have very different properties in terms of generalization and what functions can be linearly computed from them, and while a representation can use both, there's a trade-off that puts them fundamentally in tension [spya-fyxmks].

Superposition is illustrated by the "dense" code, which packs more distinct things into a representation than there are neurons — there's another kind of distributed representation that can represent all colored shapes with only 4 neurons (just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers). Such codes are sometimes called "dense". In our framing, it's maximal superposition [spya-bzhkhu]. The cost is that this compression is opaque from the outside: Dense codes like this have a very cool advantage: they can represent far more, totally unrelated objects than there are neurons. But note that there are also lots of costs to this. It isn't possible to generically select most colors or shapes with a linear probe, let alone sets [spya-xwq6ty]. The piece also notes a structural requirement for it: maximal superposition is only possible if there isn't composition. Thus, this code needs to use a non-composing set of features [spya-kq5p9m].

Why superposition matters to the argument: it's presented as one of two ways to spend a fixed representational budget, in competition with composition. The article frames this with a volume argument — If one has \(m\) bits to encode stimuli, we can think of there as being \(\exp(m)\) volume. Storing \(n\) features which arbitrarily compose together requires \(\exp(n)\) volume; so we can only store fully composable features in \(m\) bits. But if there's no composition, one can instead store \(\exp(m)\) items in superposition, although a non-linearity is required to retrieve them [spya-xcrca8], concluding that composition and superposition are two different ways to allocate the exponential volume [spya-jzkekc]. It also matters practically: superposition becomes possible specifically when features are sparse rather than dense — When features are dense (ie. combinations are common), networks can only represent one feature per neuron. But when features are sparse (combinations of many features are rare) superposition becomes possible [spya-qbuyka], with sparse "holes" in the compositional space used to store extra features [spya-ajbh7f].

The stakes for the argument as a whole are interpretability: the article's closing point is that when neural network representations are distributed in the sense we call "composition", it is possible to understand them in terms of a linear number of independent features rather than an exponential amount of volume [spya-v47ca7], and this is set against superposition, which resists that kind of linear readout. My inference is that the whole essay uses "superposition" as the name for the failure mode that makes naive interpretability methods like linear probing unreliable, since a network can pack far more concepts into a layer than it has neurons, at the cost of them not being cleanly separable — which is also why the article opens by saying this distinction matters for escaping the curse of dimensionality and understanding networks at all [spya-nwuh77].

"Monosemantic" here is being used as the opposite of "polysemantic" — a term that comes up repeatedly in Anthropic's interpretability work. A neuron (or unit) is monosemantic if it corresponds to a single, clean feature or concept, rather than firing for a jumble of unrelated things.

In this passage, the local code is described as monosemantic because there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair, and this model doesn't have any superposition. Each neuron has exactly one thing it means — "red circle," say — with no overlap or double-duty. That's precisely why the code is so wasteful: to keep every neuron single-purpose, you need one neuron per possible combination, which is why the article calls this example "silly and wasteful" a few sentences later, even while granting it useful properties.

The term matters because it sets up the contrast the whole piece is built on. Superposition is what happens when a network abandons monosemanticity to pack more features into fewer neurons than it has room for — each neuron becomes polysemantic, responding to multiple unrelated features, as seen later in the "dense" and "semi-distributed" codes. So this one word marks the baseline case — no compression, no overlap — against which composition and superposition are both, in their different ways, departures.

answers.asked: In our language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition.
answers.text:
"Monosemantic" here is the article's own term of art, contrasted with "polysemantic" — a neuron that responds to just one thing rather than many unrelated things. In this local code, each neuron stands for exactly one (shape, color) pair, so a neuron either fires for "red circle" and nothing else, or it doesn't fire at all; there's no neuron doing double duty for unrelated concepts.

"Superposition" is the specific phenomenon the whole piece is built around: representing more features than you have neurons by having neurons encode multiple, potentially unrelated things at once (which forces those features into interference with each other, retrievable only nonlinearly). Because this local code uses one neuron per pair with no overlap, it's the baseline case with zero superposition — the article is using it as the clean starting point before showing, later, how compositional and dense/superposed codes each depart from it in different directions. The wastefulness of needing a neuron for every possible pairing is exactly the cost of having no superposition at all.

answers.asked: What does "monosemantic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, "monosemantic" describes a neuron that stands for exactly one thing — it fires for one specific (shape, color) pairing and nothing else. The example is Thorpe's pure "local code," where there is a dedicated neuron for each (shape, color) pair, and Olah writes that in this setup, there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair, and in this language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition [spya-kcjqdw]. So "monosemantic" is being used as the opposite pole from "polysemantic" — a neuron that means one thing versus one that is doing double (or multiple) duty. That contrast surfaces again later when Olah describes the "semi-distributed" code, where units begin to have some meaning – they're polysemantic, but only respond to a few features [spya-vw7xv6].

Why it matters to the argument: monosemanticity is being used here as a marker of "no superposition." The local code is the baseline case — one neuron, one meaning, zero superposition — which is exactly what makes it easy to interpret but expensive in neuron count [spya-kcjqdw spya-hbmajb]. The whole essay is building toward the claim that superposition is what happens when a network gives up strict one-neuron-one-meaning monosemanticity in order to pack more features into fewer dimensions, at the cost of needing a nonlinearity to read them back out [spya-xcrca8 spya-xwq6ty]. So flagging the local code as "monosemantic" up front sets the reference point against which "polysemantic" (superposed) codes are later measured — it's the zero point on the superposition axis that lets Olah later argue composition and superposition are two separate, competing ways of being "distributed," rather than points on a single local–distributed spectrum [spya-fyxmks spya-dzemsa].
